title: Did Tutankhamun's Curse Kill 9 People? A Doctor Checked 44 Lives｜Curio Files
description:
Afternoon, November 26, 1922, Valley of the Kings. Howard Carter peers through a small hole in a wall, and Lord Carnarvon asks: can you see anything? A little over four months later, the man who asked that question was dead.

This episode starts from Carter's journal: the intact seals at the foot of the steps, the exclusive signed with The Times in January, the burial chamber opened in mid-February, a mosquito in March and a sickbed on April 5. Then how the curse got written: novelist Marie Corelli's letter of March 24, the “elemental” Arthur Conan Doyle spoke of, the canary that actually comes from a magazine article co-written with a novelist, and “death shall come on swift wings,” whose earliest traceable appearance is a 1930 newspaper. Finally, the 2002 British Medical Journal study: of the 44 Westerners on Carter's list, the 25 who went into the tomb lived to 70 on average, those who didn't to 75, with no statistical difference.

Versions that only circulate are labelled as such; where no source can be found (the Cairo blackout, the howling dog, the inscription in the tomb), we say so plainly. Sources for every number, date and quote are listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; historical figures appear as cartoon characters, unnamed and not drawn as likenesses; people who died less than seventy years ago are not depicted.

Information as of 2026-10-25

chapters.open-you: One “Can you see anything?” began a century-long curse
chapters.steps-first: Below 16 steps, the seals still intact
chapters.times-office: January: the whole tomb sold to one newspaper
chapters.bite-shave: A mosquito in March, a sickbed in April
chapters.curse-corelli: A novelist's letter, a detective writer's answer
chapters.long-carter: The man most deserving of the curse lived to 64
chapters.close-museum: 2025: 5,300 objects, a queue to see them

t001.text: You've heard it: open a pharaoh's tomb, get cursed.

t002.text: For this one tomb alone, the papers counted nine deaths.

t003.text: Afternoon, November 26, 1922, Valley of the Kings: a man pushes a candle into a fresh hole in a wall.

t004.text: The earl: can you see anything?

t005.text: He looks back and says: yes, wonderful things.

t007.text: Seven years later, a paper printed a curse said to be carved in the tomb.

t008.text: 72 years on, a doctor took the 44 Westerners in Egypt then, and tallied each one's lifespan.

t009.text: In this file, we count all 44 lives for you.

t010.text: Did people who entered Tutankhamun's tomb die sooner?

t011.text: Before that candle came 16 steps: three weeks earlier, the first was swept out of the sand.

t012.text: One step, two, down to the sixteenth, and at the bottom, a sealed door.

t013.text: The seals on that door were intact.

t014.text: He was Howard Carter, working for an earl for over a decade, and five winters in this valley had turned up almost nothing.

t015.text: Now you: the door is right there. What do you do?

t016.text: He did what you probably wouldn't: reburied the steps and cabled England.

t017.text: The man paying wasn't there. He waited in the desert over two weeks. For whom?

t018.text: The payer was Lord Carnarvon, 56, an English aristocrat.

t019.text: His money kept Carter out here, year after year, digging up air.

t020.text: He came with his daughter Evelyn, and then: the candle.

t021.text: What's in the hole? I'll show you shortly.

t022.text: Because for the next three months, the trouble wasn't the gold inside: it was the people outside.

t023.text: The first in trouble was the earl himself.

t024.text: On January 9, back in London, he signed with The Times: news from the tomb, for them alone.

t025.text: Now flip it: dozens of other papers sent reporters all the way to Egypt,

t026.text: to sit on rocks outside, seeing nothing, writing nothing. What would you do?

t027.text: An Egyptologist who studies this put it bluntly: that exclusive left a crowd of reporters sitting in the dust.

t028.text: People sitting in the dust find other stories.

t029.text: In mid-February, the burial chamber opened. This time, what was behind the door?

t030.text: Carter chiseled through a third door: behind it, a wall of gold.

t031.text: Remember that hole? Behind it, a crammed antechamber; the burial chamber lay deeper.

t032.text: This gold wall stood deeper still, a gilded shrine around a sarcophagus, big enough to nearly fill the room.

t033.text: Newspapers worldwide were waiting for word.

t034.text: Instead, the other papers could only write about outside: who went in, who quarreled, who fell ill.

t035.text: In March, a mosquito in the valley bit the earl's face.

t036.text: A bite is nothing. Then, shaving, he nicked the bump open.

t037.text: It got infected: then erysipelas, sepsis, and pneumonia.

t039.text: Evelyn sat by his bed. Was there still time?

t040.text: April 5: Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo.

t041.text: Under seven weeks after seeing that gold wall.

t042.text: In the version that circulates, Cairo blacked out that moment, and his dog in England howled and died.

t043.text: Both are just “reportedly.” And Cairo lost power all the time back then.

t044.text: But think: a man opens a pharaoh's tomb and is dead months later.

t045.text: What newspaper would pass that up?

t046.text: What's more, someone had written a letter two weeks before he died.

t047.text: The writer was Marie Corelli, once one of Britain's best-selling novelists.

t048.text: On March 24, she wrote to the press.

t049.text: She claimed she owned an ancient book saying pharaohs' tombs held “poison in boxes.”

t050.text: Whoever broke into a king's resting place took a risk. Remember those poison boxes: they'll be back.

t051.text: When the earl died, papers splashed her letter.

t052.text: The reporters in the dust finally had a story.

t053.text: On April 6, Arthur Conan Doyle, Holmes's creator, weighed in.

t054.text: He said an evil “elemental” may have killed the earl.

t055.text: If the man who wrote Sherlock Holmes says so, would readers doubt it?

t057.text: The story goes that Carter brought a canary to the valley,

t058.text: and on opening day, a cobra slid into the cage and killed it.

t059.text: You get the message right away.

t060.text: Its source: a magazine piece under Carter's name,

t062.text: It isn't from Carter's own diary.

t063.text: From that year on, whenever anyone tied to the tomb died, the papers added one more.

t065.text: Next on the list: a scholar who killed himself in England in 1924.

t066.text: It likely followed a close friend's death. The papers didn't care.

t067.text: Four years later, Carter's colleague Arthur Mace died. Not yet the one papers craved.

t068.text: He'd long since left Egypt, ill. The papers counted him anyway.

t069.text: In 1929, Carter's assistant Richard Bethell died in London, aged 46.

t070.text: This time, he wasn't the only one counted. Who else?

t071.text: Three months later, Bethell's father, Lord Westbury, jumped from the seventh-floor window of his flat.

t072.text: His note: I cannot stand any more horrors. What would the papers write?

t073.text: Remember the nine deaths from the start? On February 28, a US paper covered it and wrote: this is the ninth.

t074.text: That supposed tomb inscription ran in the same story.

t075.text: “Death shall come on swift wings to him who disturbs the peace of the king.”

t076.text: The trouble is, that line was never found in the tomb.

t077.text: Egyptologists combed every wall and object in the tomb, and found not one curse. So where did it come from?

t078.text: The earliest trace is this newspaper.

t079.text: Seven years after the tomb was opened.

t080.text: You might think: curse or not, nine deaths are real, right?

t081.text: In 1934, a museum director thought so too, and ran the numbers:

t082.text: Of the 20-odd people at the opening, six died within 12 years.

t083.text: Six: a lot? Compared to what?

t084.text: Nobody answered that seriously for another 68 years.

t085.text: Meanwhile, the papers kept ignoring one man's lifespan.

t086.text: Carter, first to look through that hole, worked in the tomb for years after.

t087.text: He died in London in 1939, aged 64, of lymphoma.

t088.text: He lived 16 more years after the chamber opened.

t089.text: And Douglas Derry, the anatomist who unwrapped the pharaoh's mummy layer by layer in 1925?

t091.text: And Evelyn, first in with her father?

t093.text: See? Those who spent longest inside and touched the most all grew old.

t095.text: To corner the curse, you put everyone from back then in one table.

t096.text: In 2002, an Australian doctor, Mark Nelson, did just that.

t097.text: Not with the papers' list, but with Carter's own.

t098.text: Remember the 44 from the start? They're the Westerners Carter logged in Egypt in the dig years.

t099.text: Of these, 25 entered the burial chamber, opened the sarcophagus, or saw the mummy.

t101.text: Compare the two groups: who died first?

t102.text: Those who went in lived to 70 on average. Those who didn't, 75.

t104.text: But too few people, too much scatter: statistically, no gap.

t105.text: The paper calls that number a p-value, 0.87. Meaning: you'd get a gap like this drawing blindfolded.

t106.text: So what on that list did affect lifespan?

t108.text: Women on the list outlived the men by 17 years. And of the group that went in, 24 were men.

t109.text: The paper's last line: no evidence supports a mummy's curse.

t110.text: It ran in the December 21 Christmas issue.

t111.text: So next time someone mentions the pharaoh's curse, ask:

t112.text: What kind of curse lets you live to old age?

t113.text: Wait, maybe you've heard another version: tomb mold, spores the earl breathed in.

t114.text: Remember Marie Corelli's poison boxes? This is the modern version.

t115.text: Its most formal source is a 2003 reader's letter in The Lancet.

t116.text: Two doctors read old reports of “facial pain,” and guessed an Aspergillus infection. The evidence?

t117.text: The journal quickly ran a rebuttal.

t118.text: And to this day, it's still just a guess.

t119.text: And remember how long Carter, who breathed the most tomb dust, lived?

t120.text: A cursing mold would have picked him first.

t121.text: Guesses aside, one thing's certain: a century later, people still fight to get in and see.

t122.text: On November 1, 2025, the Grand Egyptian Museum opened outside Cairo.

t123.text: Over 5,300 objects from this tomb are on display there. Will the people who go see them be cursed?

t124.text: Back to the opening question: did those who went in die younger?

t125.text: Remember the table? Those who went in averaged 70, those who stayed out, five years more: statistically, no difference.

t126.text: File closed. The curse was in the papers, not the tomb.

t127.text: Which movie first showed you the curse? Tell me below.

t128.text: This channel sticks to the record. Subscribe and open the files with me.
